library:
This library is a catalogue, not a review section. It lists every production car, prototype and concept the open record knows about, by marque, with a photograph wherever Wikimedia Commons holds a free one. Its job is to give a name a home: when a reader searches for an obscure coachbuilt one-off, a badge-engineered export model or a concept that never reached a showroom, the entry here says when it was introduced, who built it, and what the sourced specification looks like — and nothing more. Where the public record is silent we leave the row blank rather than fill it in.

Ownership cost and reliability verdicts live separately, in the United States ownership index, because they come from a different kind of evidence: federal complaint and recall filings, and EPA fuel-economy tests. The two sections link to each other wherever a catalogue entry matches a scored model year. To read a verdict, start with the buyer's guides, which explain what the numbers mean before you use them.
cars:
Every page in this index answers one question for one model year: what does owning this car actually cost, and what goes wrong with it? The evidence is the federal record — owner complaints and recall campaigns filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, joined to EPA fuel-economy data — normalised per year the car has been on the road so that a 2012 model is not punished for having had thirteen years in which to accumulate reports. The scoring formula is published in full on the methodology page.

A verdict only appears where the record is deep enough to support one. A model year with fewer than thirty complaints on file is shown in its model's table but does not get its own page, and a verdict built on a thin record is labelled as such. If you are shopping for a specific car, the fastest route is the finder; if you want to understand which years of a nameplate to avoid, the buyer's guides walk through the pattern year by year.
problems:
This ranking is computed, not curated. It takes every model year in the ownership dataset, divides its NHTSA complaint count by the number of years it has been on sale, and lists the twenty-five worst. Two cautions before you read it. First, complaints are filed by owners, not verified by engineers, so a viral defect can inflate a nameplate's rate for reasons that have nothing to do with the car's average reliability. Second, a very recent model year can rank high on a small number of complaints simply because it has only had a few months of exposure; the score column corrects for that with the shrinkage described in the methodology, the raw rate does not.

The pattern that repeats across the list is worth knowing: powertrain and transmission complaints cluster in the first two or three years of a new generation, and electrical complaints climb as a car ages. The buyer's guides go through the biggest nameplates one by one and say which years those clusters fall in.
stories: These are the standing rankings that MotorJury recomputes from the federal record every night: the most complained-about cars, the most recalled, the safest bets, and how electric cars actually behave in owners' hands. They change as new filings arrive, which is the point — a list nobody edits cannot be paid for. For the reasoning behind each ranking, and for written guidance on individual nameplates, read the buyer's guides, which are written by the editor and dated.
compare: Head-to-head pages put the best data-year of two natural rivals side by side. They are a shortcut into the model pages, not a substitute for them: a comparison of two nameplates hides the variation between their good and bad years, which is usually larger than the difference between the two cars.
guides: Everything on MotorJury is computed from public records, and the numbers are honest, but numbers do not tell you which year of a Honda CR-V to avoid or why a Ford Escape's complaint count jumps in 2013. These guides do. Each one is written and signed by the editor, dated, and built on the same NHTSA and EPA record the rest of the site uses, so every claim can be checked against the model pages it links to. They are revised when the data moves.
